ui.landingPage.faq.label: Frequently asked questions
ui.landingPage.faq.heading: Questions, answered with sources.
ui.landingPage.faq.note: Practical notes, not medical advice. Each answer lists where it comes from.
ui.landingPage.faq.items.1.a: For a machine, yes. Use CPAP therapy only if you have a prescription from your doctor or nurse practitioner. Your prescription covers your equipment and your settings. Each machine must be set for the person using it. APAP and bilevel machines are more complex, and a sleep specialist should prescribe them. {machineLine} {rxMaskLine} Only trained professionals should change your machine’s settings, and Liivv never advises on them. In Ontario, it’s your right to choose your community respiratory therapy provider.
ui.landingPage.faq.items.1.machineLine: Liivv doesn’t sell CPAP or other sleep apnea machines yet.
ui.landingPage.faq.items.1.rxMaskLine: On Liivv, a complete mask, including a children’s mask, needs a CPAP prescription, which a Liivv pharmacist checks before your order ships. Parts and supplies, such as cushions, headgear, tubing and filters, go straight in your cart.
ui.landingPage.faq.items.2.q: Can I take my CPAP on a plane?
ui.landingPage.faq.items.2.a: Yes. A CPAP machine is allowed in your carry-on and in checked baggage. Bring it as carry-on when you fly. At security, you can either put it in a clear plastic bag you bring for screening, or leave the tubes and mask in the case and put only the main unit in a bin. The distilled water it uses is exempt from the liquid limits. You don’t need a document about your medical needs, but you can show one to the screening officer if you think it will help. For a packing list, go to <link>Travelling with CPAP</link>.
ui.landingPage.faq.items.3.q: How often should I replace my mask and filter?
ui.landingPage.faq.items.3.a: Follow the manual for your machine and mask first. General advice differs, so here it is side by side. Most machines are replaced every 3 to 5 years, and accessories every 3 to 12 months. Change the machine’s filter every 2 months, or as needed. Check your tubing and headgear, and replace them when they’re worn. Programs also set the most they cover. NIHB’s guidelines, for example, are up to 14 inlet filters a year, 2 a year for each type of mask with headgear (face, nasal or nasal pillow), and 2 a year for tubing. More may be considered case by case, with prior approval. If a plan pays for your equipment, check its replacement time frames before you order. For signs a part is worn, go to <link>Time to replace supplies</link>.
ui.landingPage.faq.items.4.q: What if my machine or mask is recalled?
ui.landingPage.faq.items.4.a: Each recall notice says what to do, so look up your model on the Government of Canada’s <link>recalls and safety alerts</link> site. For the 2021 recall of some Philips machines made before April 26, 2021, the advice was to talk to your doctor or medical device provider before you stop or change how you use your machine. Canadian specialist advice for people using these machines for sleep apnea was to contact their doctor soon and keep using the machine in the meantime. For those machines, the advice was also to stop ozone and UV cleaning, and to clean the machine only as the maker’s instructions say. Some masks have magnets that can affect some metal implants and devices, such as pacemakers, in you or in someone who lives with you, cares for you or shares your bed. For the masks in one 2022 advisory, the advice is to stop using the mask if anyone in that group has one of the listed implants. For other masks, check with the mask’s maker and your health care team. Read the warning in <link>Driving & Staying Safe</link>.

chapters.is-it-sleep-apnea.title: Is It Sleep Apnea?
chapters.is-it-sleep-apnea.heroBody: Snoring, gasping, always tired? Here are the signs, how testing works in Canada, and what your results mean.
chapters.is-it-sleep-apnea.focus: The signs: what sleep apnea is, what others notice, how common it is, a checklist to take to your doctor, and two signposts, for trouble sleeping and for snoring. Getting tested: talking to your doctor, lab and home tests, reading your results, what happens next, and who to ask.
chapters.is-it-sleep-apnea.vibe: Clear and unhurried: what to notice, and what to ask.
chapters.is-it-sleep-apnea.categoriesInt: Only a sleep study can tell
This chapter helps you notice the signs and talk to your doctor about them. It can’t tell you whether you have sleep apnea. A sleep study does that.
Sleep apnea means short pauses in your breathing while you sleep
A pause usually lasts 10 to 30 seconds. Then your brain wakes you just enough to take a breath. Most people don’t remember waking
Obstructive sleep apnea is the most common type. Your airway narrows or closes while you sleep, even though your body keeps trying to breathe
Central sleep apnea is less common. Your airway is open, but your brain doesn’t send the signal to breathe
Untreated, sleep apnea can lead to daytime sleepiness and trouble thinking clearly. It raises the risk of car crashes, high blood pressure, heart attack and stroke
Sleep apnea can be treated. Your Treatment Options covers the choices
Children can have sleep apnea too. In the day, it can show up as trouble concentrating, hyperactivity or irritability. See This Might Be You.
A bed partner or family member often notices the signs before you do
Many people with sleep apnea don’t know they snore or gasp at night
Pauses in breathing, then a gasp or a choke
What a bed partner has seen or heard helps your doctor. If you sleep alone, your doctor can still check for signs
If someone tells you they’ve noticed this, mention it to your doctor. The checklist below prints a list to take with you.
What they may hear or see
In 2016 and 2017, 6.4% of Canadians said a health professional had diagnosed them with sleep apnea
Among people aged 60 to 79, it was 12.8%, about three times as common as in younger adults
Men were twice as likely as women to report a diagnosis
Women’s signs are more often tiredness or trouble sleeping, and men’s more often snoring. So sleep apnea may be missed more often in women
Nearly a third of Canadian adults (30%) were at moderate or high risk, based on a short questionnaire and body measurements
Many people have sleep apnea without knowing it. In population studies, 86% to 95% of people with significant sleep apnea had never been diagnosed
If any of this sounds like you, the checklist below can help you talk to your doctor.
Signs to mention to your doctor
Signs vary
Signs vary from person to person. Being very sleepy during the day is the most common one
Women’s signs are more often tiredness or trouble sleeping. Men’s are more often snoring
Signs to mention
Someone has heard you snore loudly, most nights
Someone has seen you stop breathing, gasp or choke in your sleep
You’re very sleepy during the day, and you don’t know why
You feel tired or worn out much of the time
You wake up with headaches
You wake up often in the night, or get up to pee
Your sleep doesn’t leave you feeling rested
You find it hard to concentrate or remember things
You feel irritable or low
You have high blood pressure
You’ve nodded off, or nearly, while driving
Things that raise the chance
Anyone of any age can get sleep apnea
It’s more likely if you’re male or over 40
It’s more likely if it runs in your family
It’s more likely with a large, thick neck or a lot of extra weight, or with large tonsils or a recessed chin

Not a diagnostic tool. These are signs to mention, not a test. Having some doesn’t mean you have sleep apnea, and signs vary, so a short list doesn’t rule it out. A sleep study is how it’s diagnosed. If you’ve nodded off, or nearly, while driving, read Driving & Staying Safe now.
Tick any that fit you
Questions to bring to your doctor
Could these signs be sleep apnea, or something else?
Do I need a sleep study? In a lab, or at home?
How long is the wait, and who will contact me?
Is it safe for me to drive while I wait?
Will the kind of test matter for funding later?
Trouble falling asleep, staying asleep or waking too early, with distress or daytime problems for 3 months or more, is called insomnia disorder
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is the first-line treatment, before sleeping pills
CBT-I is usually 4 to 8 sessions with a trained clinician, in person or by video. Some people start with a self-guided program, online or from a book
Sleepwell, a not-for-profit program led from Dalhousie University, has CBT-I tools such as a sleep diary
Poor sleep can also come from sleep apnea. A sleep study may be needed if your doctor suspects it
Adults aged 18 to 64 need 7 to 9 hours of sleep a night. Adults 65 and older need 7 to 8
This site doesn’t cover insomnia in depth. Your doctor or nurse practitioner can assess it with you.
Talk to your doctor or nurse practitioner
Sleepwell is a not-for-profit program led from Dalhousie University.
Loud snoring is a sign that your airway is partly blocked as you sleep
International guidance: most people with sleep apnea snore, but not everyone who snores has sleep apnea
Snoring with pauses in breathing, gasping or choking is a reason to see your doctor
So is snoring along with daytime sleepiness or tiredness, especially if you also have high blood pressure
Children can snore without having sleep apnea too. Signs and testing for children are in This Might Be You
Only a sleep study can tell snoring from sleep apnea. The checklist above can help you talk to your doctor.
If you think you have sleep apnea, see your family doctor or nurse practitioner
Expect questions about your sleep, your daytime sleepiness and your health, and a look at your nose, mouth and throat
You may be asked to fill in a short questionnaire about daytime sleepiness
Expect to be asked whether you drive for work or have a safety-critical job, and about any near misses at the wheel
Then your doctor orders a home sleep test or refers you to a sleep clinic. How this works differs by province

Waits can be long. The Canadian target (2011) is testing within 4 weeks of referral for suspected severe sleep apnea, a safety-critical job or some serious health conditions, and within 6 months for everyone
In a 2009 survey, nearly 1 in 4 adults (23%) who had been told they had sleep apnea had never been referred for an overnight sleep test

Funding programs can have rules about testing. In Ontario, funding for a machine through the Assistive Devices Program starts with a doctor at an ADP-registered sleep clinic. The Non-Insured Health Benefits program doesn’t pay for sleep tests. Funding & Coverage has the details for your province.
An in-lab sleep study (polysomnography, or Level 1) is an overnight test in a sleep lab
Small wires on your head, face, chest and legs record your brain activity, breathing and oxygen as you sleep. Staff watch through the night
It’s the standard test. It can find every type of sleep apnea, and other sleep problems
A home sleep apnea test is a small device you wear overnight in your own bed, after someone shows you how to put it on
It records your breathing, oxygen and pulse. It can’t measure sleep, so it’s less sensitive than a lab study
It checks only for obstructive sleep apnea, in adults with symptoms whose doctor thinks it’s likely
Home tests aren’t for checking people who have no symptoms
A negative or unclear home test doesn’t rule out sleep apnea. If your doctor still suspects it, a lab study is the next step
Overnight oximetry, a clip that measures oxygen and pulse, isn’t enough on its own to diagnose sleep apnea

Your doctor chooses the test. Serious heart or lung disease, a past stroke, other sleep problems, regular opioid use and some other conditions mean a home test isn’t the right test. Your doctor refers you to a sleep specialist instead
For children, an overnight lab study is the standard. A home test is a second choice, only for healthy children over 5 who can’t get a lab study. More in This Might Be You.
Your sleep study report says whether you have sleep apnea, and whether it’s mild, moderate or severe
The main number is the AHI (apnea-hypopnea index): how many times an hour your breathing stops or becomes shallow
Mild is 5 to 14 an hour, moderate is 15 to 29, and severe is 30 or more
The AHI isn’t the whole picture. Your sleep doctor also weighs your symptoms, your health and your job
Treatment may be suggested even when the AHI is mild, if you’re tired or sleepy
Once you’re on CPAP, the machine shows “events per hour”. It’s a useful daily guide, but not a true AHI. Ask your sleep team what yours means
This scale helps you read a report, not test yourself. Your sleep doctor goes over your results with you.
AHI: breathing events per hour of sleep
These bands are for adults (19 and over).
Your sleep doctor also weighs your symptoms and your health.
chapters.is-it-sleep-apnea.categories.10: A sleep doctor or your own doctor reads your results, makes the diagnosis and suggests a treatment
The choice depends on how severe it is, your symptoms, your health and your job
CPAP is generally the most effective treatment. A machine blows a steady stream of air through a mask, to keep your airway open

Other options include an oral appliance for mild to moderate sleep apnea. Healthy eating, exercise and weight loss are recommended for people who carry extra weight, but they aren’t enough on their own if you’re sleepy or your sleep apnea is moderate or severe. Your Treatment Options covers each one
You need a prescription for CPAP. Your prescriber sets your settings
Expect follow-up: soon after you start, to check the treatment is working, then over the long term
Starting CPAP walks you through setup and the first weeks.
chapters.is-it-sleep-apnea.categories.11: Your family doctor or nurse practitioner: your symptoms, a home test or a referral
A sleep doctor (sleep specialist): your diagnosis, how severe it is, and your treatment
A registered respiratory therapist (RRT): choosing and using your equipment, once your treatment is prescribed
Sleepy at the wheel, or nodded off while driving: read Driving & Staying Safe now
Not sure where to start? Start with your family doctor or nurse practitioner.

chapters.staying-safe.title: Driving & Staying Safe
chapters.staying-safe.heroBody: Sleepiness and driving, who decides about your licence, and how to keep your machine and mask safe. The signs that can’t wait come first.
chapters.staying-safe.focus: On the road: why sleepiness matters, who decides if you can drive, what’s checked for each licence class, and driving while treatment starts. Your device: recalls, masks with magnets, cleaning, buying safely, choosing a supplier, reporting a problem, and who to call.
chapters.staying-safe.vibe: Calm and direct: clear steps for the moments that matter.
chapters.staying-safe.categoriesIntro.ey: On the road, or about your device?
chapters.staying-safe.categoriesIntro.bo: This chapter explains the rules and the safety steps. Your doctor and your licensing authority make the decisions about driving. Only your sleep team changes your treatment.
chapters.staying-safe.urgent.heading: Stop and act now
chapters.staying-safe.urgent.intro: Most of this chapter can wait. These can’t.
chapters.staying-safe.urgent.tiers.emerg: Call 911 or your local emergency number right away for:
Chest pain or discomfort, or other signs of a heart attack
Signs of a stroke: a drooping face, not being able to raise both arms, or slurred or jumbled speech
Someone who has passed out, can’t be woken up, or is confused
A child with severe trouble breathing, chest pain, blue lips or fingertips, or who is confused or not responding as usual. Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department right away
Stop now, then tell your doctor

You fell asleep at the wheel, or nearly did, or had a crash because you were sleepy. Stop driving now and tell your doctor. You may also need to tell your licensing authority. Don’t drive again until your sleep apnea is treated and you’re told you can
Not an emergency, but don’t wait

You, or someone who sleeps near you, notice pauses in breathing, gasping or choking in your sleep. Talk to your doctor or health care provider as soon as you can. If someone can’t be woken up, call 911
chapters.staying-safe.urgent.note: Snoring and long pauses in breathing while a child sleeps can be signs of sleep apnea. Talk to your child’s health-care provider. Chapter 06 covers children.
chapters.staying-safe.startHere.heading: On the road, or about your device?
chapters.staying-safe.categories.1.title: Sleepiness and driving
chapters.staying-safe.categories.1.items: Untreated sleep apnea raises your risk of a car crash
The main sign is being sleepier than expected during the day
Most people with sleep apnea never have a crash. The risk is still higher
Your doctor may ask your licence class, and whether your work is one where sleepiness could be a hazard
Your doctor may also ask if you’ve fallen asleep at the wheel or come close in the past 5 years, and about any crashes or near misses when sleepy
chapters.staying-safe.categories.1.note: A driver with sleep apnea can be found fit to drive again, based on their symptoms and on showing they use their treatment. If you’ve been sleepy at the wheel, see “Stop now, then tell your doctor” at the top of this page.
chapters.staying-safe.categories.2.title: Who decides if you can drive
chapters.staying-safe.categories.2.items: Your doctor assesses whether you’re medically fit to drive
The licensing authority where you live decides whether you can hold a licence. Driving safety is a provincial matter, not a federal one
How severe your sleep apnea is doesn’t decide it on its own. Sleepiness, other health conditions, medicines, your sleep schedule and past crashes count too
The rules differ from province to province

In Ontario, doctors and nurse practitioners must report sleep apnea that is untreated or not successfully treated, with an AHI of 30 or more and daytime sleepiness. A mandatory report leads to a licence suspension
In BC, drivers with sleep apnea have a licence condition: stop driving and report any episode of sleep at the wheel to their doctor and to RoadSafetyBC
chapters.staying-safe.categories.2.note: AHI is the number of breathing pauses and shallow breaths per hour of sleep. Chapter 01 explains it. Ask your doctor how the rules apply to you.
chapters.staying-safe.categories.3.title: What’s checked, by licence class
chapters.staying-safe.categories.3.items: Every class: severe sleep apnea (AHI 30 or more) rules out driving unless it’s successfully treated, or a sleep specialist finds a low risk of a sleep-related crash
Every class: after a crash from falling asleep or sleepiness in the past 5 years, you must show your sleep apnea is successfully treated
In BC, treatment is checked with a full download from your CPAP or bilevel machine prepared by a respiratory therapist, or with a sleep study
Every class, if you use CPAP: machine records showing use of at least 4 hours a night, on more than 70% of nights, over at least 30 days
Private licences: your sleep doctor or your family doctor can confirm you’re fit to drive again
Commercial licences: the checks are stricter than for private drivers. Commercial drivers should ideally be seen at a sleep centre within 4 weeks of referral
Commercial licences: after a crash from falling asleep, or excessive sleepiness while driving, stop driving now until sleep tests are done and treatment works
chapters.staying-safe.categories.3.note: These are licensing measures, not health targets. Your sleep team sets your own goal. Never change your machine’s settings to change your numbers.
chapters.staying-safe.categories.3.figur: These are licensing measures, not health targets. Your sleep team sets your own goal.
Your licensing authority makes the decision. Rules differ by province.
chapters.staying-safe.categories.4.title: While you start treatment
chapters.staying-safe.categories.4.items: While treatment starts, you may be able to keep driving if you aren’t sleepy while driving and haven’t had a crash from falling asleep. Ask your doctor
If you have been sleepy at the wheel or had a sleep-related crash, driving can start again once you use your treatment well and the sleepiness is gone
Your machine records how many hours and days you use it. Your doctor, an insurer or a licensing authority may ask for this report
Once treatment works, driving safely is your responsibility. Have your treatment reviewed from time to time by your doctor or sleep specialist, for example at least every 5 years
If sleepiness at the wheel comes back, stop driving and tell your doctor
chapters.staying-safe.categories.4.note: Your machine’s settings are changed only by trained professionals. If your treatment isn’t working, call your sleep team.
chapters.staying-safe.categories.5.title: Recalls: what to do
chapters.staying-safe.categories.5.items: In 2021, Philips Respironics recalled several models of CPAP and bilevel machines. Sound-reducing foam inside them could break down, and particles could get into the air you breathe
If your machine is recalled, don’t stop or change your therapy before you talk to your doctor or equipment provider
Don’t try to remove or replace the foam yourself
Clean the machine only the way the maker’s instructions say. Ozone cleaning may make the foam break down faster
Some masks with magnets have also been recalled. See the next card
chapters.staying-safe.categories.5.note: The maker planned to close its registration portal at the end of December 2024, and to finish its repair and replacement program in Canada by the end of June 2025. If you still use an affected machine, talk to your doctor or equipment provider.
chapters.staying-safe.categories.6.title: Masks with magnets
chapters.staying-safe.categories.6.items: Some CPAP masks have magnets in the clips or straps that hold the headgear on
Close to some metal implants and medical devices, a magnet may affect how they work or move them out of place. This could cause serious injury, or even death
It matters for everyone close to the mask: you, the people you live with, caregivers and bed partners

Implants that magnets may affect include pacemakers, defibrillators (ICDs), nerve stimulators (including hypoglossal nerve stimulators), brain fluid shunts, aneurysm clips, embolic coils, metal stents, implanted ports and pumps such as insulin pumps, hearing implants with a magnet such as cochlear implants, and metal in the eye. The full list is longer

What to do depends on the mask and on the implant. If you, or anyone close to the mask, has an implant or metal in their body, check with the mask’s maker and with your health care team about that implant before you use a mask with magnets

Some masks are named in Health Canada notices. For the masks in the 2022 public advisory, the advice is to stop using the mask if anyone close to it has one of the listed implants, and to get a mask without magnets. For an implant that isn’t on the list, keep the mask at least 15 cm (6 inches) away from it
For the masks in the 2022 advisory: if no one close to the mask has a metal implant or metal object in their body, you can keep using it
chapters.staying-safe.categories.6.note: Not sure whether your mask has magnets? Check its instructions, or ask its maker. You can also look up your mask on the Government of Canada’s <link>recalls and safety alerts</link> site.
chapters.staying-safe.categories.7.title: Cleaning the approved way
chapters.staying-safe.categories.7.items: Clean your machine and mask only the way the maker’s instructions say
For the machines in the 2021 Philips recall, the advice was to stop using cleaning methods the maker hasn’t approved, such as ozone or UV-light cleaners
Ozone cleaning can speed up the breakdown of the foam inside some machines
Breathing ozone may affect how well your lungs work. UV light may badly burn skin and eyes
There isn’t enough evidence that all ozone and UV devices sold to kill germs are safe to use, or that they work
chapters.staying-safe.categories.7.note: Everyday cleaning with pure soap and warm water is in Chapter 05.
chapters.staying-safe.categories.8.title: Buying a device safely
chapters.staying-safe.categories.8.items: Use CPAP only if you have a prescription from your doctor
Auto (APAP) and bilevel machines are more complex, and should be prescribed only by a sleep specialist
PAP machines sold in Canada must have a Health Canada medical device licence. You can check a device in the Medical Devices Active Licence Listing (MDALL)
Buying online can mean getting a device that is unlicensed, recalled or fake
Don’t buy from a website that won’t give a street address or a working phone number
Second-hand equipment: make sure it’s clean and works as it should. Every machine must be set for the person using it
chapters.staying-safe.categories.8.note: Ask your health care provider whether a device is right for you before you buy, and follow up afterwards to check it fits and works.
chapters.staying-safe.categories.9.title: Choosing a supplier
chapters.staying-safe.categories.9.items: Choose a supplier with a registered respiratory therapist or a registered sleep technologist to guide you
A good supplier fits your mask, lets you try masks, and helps if you have trouble
New users can expect follow-up at about 7 days, an overnight oxygen test at 2 to 4 weeks, and check-ins at 30 and 60 days with a review of your machine’s data

In Ontario, you have the right to choose your community respiratory therapy provider. A respiratory therapist must tell you that you can choose another supplier, and that your care won’t suffer if you do
Many machines store your data on servers outside Canada, where privacy laws may be different. Ask your supplier how your data is handled
chapters.staying-safe.categories.9.note: Bring the questions below when you choose a supplier.
chapters.staying-safe.categories.9.figur: Who will fit my mask, and are they a respiratory therapist or sleep technologist?
Can I try masks, and what is your exchange policy?
When will you follow up with me?
Where is my machine’s data stored, and who can see it?
Is this device licensed by Health Canada?
chapters.staying-safe.categories.10.item: A device problem includes a device that fails, or stops working as well as it should
Everyone who has a problem with a medical device, or sees one, is strongly encouraged to report it to Health Canada
Consumers can report online with Health Canada’s consumer form
Your health care provider can help you report, and may add details that help the review
You can also report side effects or complaints about a recalled device to Health Canada
chapters.staying-safe.categories.10.note: If the problem has made you unwell, call your doctor first.
chapters.staying-safe.categories.11.item: Your doctor or sleep specialist: sleepiness at the wheel, fitness to drive, a recalled machine, a mask with magnets near an implant, or treatment that isn’t working
Your licensing authority: questions about your licence and the rules where you live
Your equipment provider: mask fit, how your equipment works, cleaning, and follow-up
Health Canada: report a problem with a medical device

Call 911: chest pain, signs of a stroke, trouble breathing, someone who has passed out or can’t be woken up, or anyone hurt in a crash. 911, or the nearest emergency department: a child with severe trouble breathing, chest pain, blue lips or fingertips, or who is confused or not responding as usual
chapters.staying-safe.categories.11.figu: 911 (for a child, 911 or the emergency department)
chapters.staying-safe.programsBand.cards: PAP machines sold in Canada must have a Health Canada licence. Search the device in MDALL.
If it is, don’t stop or change your therapy before you talk to your doctor or equipment provider.
If your mask has magnets and anyone close to you has a metal implant, check with your health care team and the mask’s maker. If a Health Canada notice for your mask says to stop using it, stop.
Clean it only the way the maker’s instructions say.
chapters.staying-safe.closing.heading: Safe on the road, safe at home
chapters.staying-safe.closing.body: Use your treatment, know who decides about driving, and check your equipment: licensed, not recalled, magnets checked if anyone close to you has an implant, cleaned the approved way.
chapters.staying-safe.governance.disclai: This is general information, not medical or legal advice. Your doctor assesses your fitness to drive, and your licensing authority decides. Only your prescriber decides your treatment and settings, and only trained professionals change them. Liivv never advises on machine settings.

chapters.treatment-options.title: Your Treatment Options
chapters.treatment-options.heroBody: A breathing machine, a mouth device, or changes to everyday habits: what each one is, who it suits, and what to ask before you choose.
chapters.treatment-options.focus: Breathing machines: CPAP and APAP, bilevel, central and complex sleep apnea, travel machines, and renting, trying or buying. Without a machine: oral appliances, weight and everyday habits, comparing your options, shop fixes and new treatments, and who to ask.
chapters.treatment-options.vibe: Clear and even-handed: every option, with its trade-offs.
chapters.treatment-options.categoriesInt: The right treatment is the one you can use every night

Your sleep team chooses your treatment with you, based on your sleep test and your health. This chapter explains the options so you can ask good questions. Liivv never advises on machine settings. For a child, see This Might Be You.
chapters.treatment-options.startHere.hea: A breathing machine, or another way?
CPAP and APAP: the usual first treatment
CPAP is generally the most effective treatment for obstructive sleep apnea
A machine blows a steady stream of air through a tube into a mask. The air holds your airway open while you sleep
CPAP gives one steady pressure all night. APAP (auto CPAP) changes the pressure through the night as your breathing changes
You need a prescription. Your prescriber sets the pressure, and only trained professionals should change the machine’s settings
Each machine is set for the person using it. Using a machine set for someone else could harm your health
CPAP is a treatment, not a cure. It only works on the nights you use it

Fixed CPAP is the main treatment. APAP is an alternative, but not for people with heart or lung disease, nerve or muscle disease, or breathing problems in sleep that aren’t only obstructive, such as central sleep apnea. APAP is more complex than CPAP, and some guidance says only a sleep specialist should prescribe it. Your prescriber decides which one you get.
A bilevel machine gives a higher pressure when you breathe in and a lower pressure when you breathe out
For obstructive sleep apnea, the main reason to use one is comfort: some people find it easier to breathe out against a lower pressure
Bilevel machines are more complex than CPAP. They should be prescribed only by a sleep specialist
Bilevel is also used for some other breathing problems in sleep, when oxygen and carbon dioxide levels don’t improve with CPAP
Government funding may help some people pay for bilevel. Ask your sleep team, and see Paying for it
Canadian guidance differs on when bilevel is used for obstructive sleep apnea. Your sleep specialist decides whether it’s right for you.
Central and complex sleep apnea: a specialist’s call
In central sleep apnea, the throat and airway are normal. The brain doesn’t send the signal to breathe
It is common in people with heart failure, atrial fibrillation or other heart conditions, people taking opioids, and people with some neurological conditions
Standard PAP machines are not meant to be the only treatment for central sleep apnea. Used alone, they can make it worse
If central sleep apnea is suspected, it should be checked with a detailed overnight sleep test in an accredited sleep lab, to find the right treatment
Treating the other condition, such as heart failure, can improve central sleep apnea

Some people start having central pauses after they begin CPAP. This is called complex sleep apnea, and it can happen in up to 10% of people treated with CPAP. If it happens to you, talk with your doctor about continuing PAP

Some newer machines, such as adaptive servo-ventilation (ASV), are used for central sleep apnea. In 2015, Health Canada posted a Type I recall of several ASV machines: a serious safety concern was found in people with symptomatic, chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, whose risk of cardiovascular death was 33.5% higher on ASV. ASV is a sleep specialist’s decision. If you have heart failure, make sure your sleep specialist knows.
Smaller travel machines are easy to carry, quiet, and can run on batteries
The trade-offs: the pressure may not stay as steady, batteries cost extra where there’s no power outlet, and they may not humidify the air enough
Altitude can change how a machine works, unless it adjusts for it. Tell your provider if you live in, or often travel to, places much higher or lower than where your pressure was set
Most machines can also run on a battery pack, a car adapter or a marine battery adapter
A travel machine still needs a prescription, set by your prescriber for you
Keep using your treatment when you travel. Flying? See Everyday Liivving for taking your machine on board
Talk to your prescriber and equipment provider before you choose a travel machine, so it fits your prescription and the way you travel.
You can buy or rent CPAP equipment
Ask about a trial. Some suppliers offer equipment trials, and some won’t take back or refund equipment once it has been used
If you end up needing a different machine, an extended health insurer may refuse to pay for a second one. That’s one more reason a trial matters
Look for a supplier with a registered respiratory therapist or a registered polysomnographic technologist to support you
Equipment bought in Canada usually has a 3-year warranty. Ask about warranty, how long repairs take, and whether you get a loaner in the meantime
Every PAP machine sold in Canada needs a Health Canada medical device licence. You can check a machine in Health Canada’s licence list
A second-hand machine is hard to judge. It may not work well, and the warranty may be gone
You can choose your supplier. In Ontario, respiratory therapists must tell you that you can pick another provider or product, and that your care won’t suffer if you do

Whoever you buy from, online or in person: if you’re new to PAP, look for a provider who shows you how to use your equipment, teaches you about PAP therapy and checks in with you regularly. If you buy online, choose a company that asks for your prescription first. Some local providers won’t help with equipment bought online.
An oral appliance fits over your teeth. It holds your lower jaw and tongue forward so they don’t block your airway
It may suit mild to moderate sleep apnea, or people who can’t use or don’t want CPAP
Get a medical assessment first, to confirm sleep apnea and how severe it is. Your dentist should work with your doctor
See a dentist with experience fitting these devices. For people it works for, a custom device can work as well as CPAP and is often easier to put up with
Adjustable devices are better than fixed ones. Devices with rigid bars or screws likely work better than ones with elastic straps
Boil-and-bite devices are not recommended for treating sleep apnea. They are much less effective and more likely to cause problems
Jaw or tooth pain, chewing trouble and some tooth movement can happen. Tell your dentist if it isn’t comfortable
After you start, your doctor may order a follow-up sleep test to check it’s working
An oral appliance is a medical treatment, not a store-bought snoring guard. Your sleep team and your dentist decide together if it’s right for you.
Mild sleep apnea with overweight or obesity: lifestyle changes are the recommended treatment
Mild sleep apnea without overweight: active treatment isn’t routinely recommended. But treatment should be considered if you’re tired or sleepy, even when it’s mild
Healthy habits help, but on their own they aren’t enough if you’re sleepy or have moderate or severe sleep apnea
Losing weight can shrink the tissue around your airway. People who lose 10% of their weight can have a 30% decrease in their symptoms
Weight loss works better if you keep using your treatment while you lose weight, then get retested once you reach your goal
Alcohol and sedatives (medicines that make you sleepy) can relax your throat muscles too much and let your airway close. Avoiding them may help keep it open
Smoking can make your nose stuffy and irritated, which can get in the way of CPAP
Lifestyle changes don’t work for everyone, and may not work forever. If your symptoms come back, see your doctor
If you gain or lose 30 pounds (about 14 kg) or more, go back to your sleep specialist. Your pressure may need to be checked
Habits work alongside your treatment, not instead of it, unless your sleep team says so. Don’t stop a treatment or a prescribed medicine without talking to your doctor.
Moderate or severe sleep apnea: CPAP is the recommended treatment. If CPAP isn’t acceptable to you, an oral appliance is recommended
Mild sleep apnea: lifestyle changes if you’re overweight. CPAP or an oral appliance are also options
CPAP has the largest effect on how severe sleep apnea is

A jaw-advancing oral appliance has roughly a 70% chance of working in mild sleep apnea. In moderate sleep apnea it has about a 50% chance of fully working, and in severe about 40%. In moderate and severe, the chances are lower with a BMI over 35
Every treatment takes getting used to. Using it every night, all night, is what makes it work
Whatever you choose, follow-up continues until your breathing pauses are back to normal: fewer than 5 an hour
Tongue-retaining devices are only for snoring or very mild sleep apnea
Your sleep team decides with you, based on your sleep test, your health and what you can use every night.
Shop fixes and new treatments: check first
Nasal strips and nasal dilators may help air flow through your nose. They don’t treat the blockage in your throat that causes sleep apnea
A chin strap on its own doesn’t fix the blockage either. A badly fitted strap can push the jaw back and make the blockage worse
Boil-and-bite mouthguards are not recommended for treating sleep apnea
There are many experimental treatments. Before you try one, ask your sleep specialist about the risks and benefits for you
Snoring can be a sign of sleep apnea. If you’re treating snoring on your own, get checked first.

A dentist with experience in oral appliances: after your medical assessment
Your equipment provider’s respiratory therapist: set-up, mask fit, and trouble getting used to your machine
Your doctor: if your symptoms come back, or your weight changes by 30 pounds or more

A dentist with oral appliance experience
Ask your prescriber why they chose it for you, and what else could work.
Ask about trials, whether used equipment can be returned, and what your insurer will pay for.
Look for a registered respiratory therapist or polysomnographic technologist, and check-ins in the first weeks.
Every PAP machine sold in Canada needs a Health Canada medical device licence. You can look it up.

chapters.starting-cpap.title: Starting CPAP
chapters.starting-cpap.heroBody: Getting set up and getting used to it: your prescription, your mask, water for the humidifier, the first nights, and who to call when something isn’t right.
chapters.starting-cpap.focus: Your setup: follow-up, your prescription, mask types, fit, the humidifier and a starter list. The first weeks: first nights, what your usage numbers mean, fixes for common problems, and what to do if it isn’t working.
chapters.starting-cpap.vibe: Practical and patient. Most problems have a fix, and you don’t have to solve them alone.
chapters.starting-cpap.categoriesIntro.b: This chapter helps you follow the plan your sleep team made with you. Your prescriber sets your pressure. Liivv never advises on settings. If your team told you something different, follow your team.
chapters.starting-cpap.startHere.heading: Getting set up, or getting used to it?
chapters.starting-cpap.categories.1.item: Wherever you get your equipment, online or in person, a good start includes a mask fitting, help using your machine, and someone who follows up to see how your therapy is going
About 7 days in: a check on mask comfort, the airflow, leaks, how often you use it, and any feeling of being closed in
At 2 to 4 weeks: an overnight oxygen test while you use CPAP, to check your oxygen level is normal on treatment
At 30 and 60 days: the same questions, plus how you sleep and feel, and a look at your machine’s data to see if treatment is working
After that: a follow-up at least once a year, with your machine’s data and a check of your mask and tubing
chapters.starting-cpap.categories.1.note: This schedule comes from Canadian provincial guidance for people new to CPAP. It’s shown here for every province. Your sleep team may set a different one. If so, follow theirs.
chapters.starting-cpap.categories.2.item: You need a prescription for CPAP. It comes after a medical assessment and a sleep test
Your prescription says what pressure your machine is set to. For insurance, it should also name your mask and humidifier
Auto-adjusting machines (APAP) and bilevel machines are more complex. A sleep specialist should prescribe them
Only trained professionals should change your machine’s settings. Don’t change them yourself
A machine is set for one person. Using a machine set for someone else could harm your health

Ask your prescriber about your pressure if your weight goes up or down by 30 pounds or more, or if you move to, or often travel to, a much higher or lower place. If you’re told you have central sleep apnea, talk to your doctor about whether to keep using CPAP
Every CPAP machine sold in Canada must have a medical device licence. You can look a machine up in Health Canada’s online licence list
In Ontario, respiratory therapists must tell you that you can choose a different provider or product
chapters.starting-cpap.categories.2.note: Liivv never advises on pressure or settings. Questions about them go to your prescriber or your respiratory therapist.
chapters.starting-cpap.categories.3.titl: Mask types to ask your RT about
chapters.starting-cpap.categories.3.item: Nasal pillows sit at the openings of your nostrils
A nasal mask fits over your nose
A full-face mask covers your nose and mouth
A child is fitted for a mask made for children (a paediatric mask), not an adult one

Some masks have magnets in the clips or straps. If you, or anyone you live or sleep near, has an implant or metal device that magnets can affect, such as a pacemaker, tell your RT before you choose a mask. Already using a mask with magnets? Check with the mask’s maker and your health care team about the implant
chapters.starting-cpap.categories.3.note: The right mask is the one that fits you and feels comfortable. It can make a big difference to how well CPAP works, and to whether you keep using it. These are general patterns, not a fitting. Try masks on with your RT.
chapters.starting-cpap.categories.3.figu: What sounds like you?
I breathe through my mouth
I breathe through my nose
I feel closed in easily
I have a beard or moustache
I move around a lot in my sleep
My nose is often stuffy or blocked
I don’t want anything inside my nose

Nasal pillows
Nasal mask
Full-face mask
A full-face mask may suit people who breathe through their mouth. So may a nasal mask with a chin strap.
Nasal masks and nasal pillows may suit people who breathe mainly through their nose.
Nasal pillows or a nasal mask may feel less closed in. Some people feel closed in with a full-face mask.
Nasal pillows may suit people with facial hair.
Nasal pillows may suit people who move around in their sleep. A chin strap may help keep a mask on.
A full-face mask may suit people whose nose is often stuffy or blocked.
If you don’t want anything inside your nose, a nasal mask may suit you better than pillows.
With a high, narrow nose bridge, nasal pillows may leak less than other masks.

Clean your mask every day. Wash it with pure soap and warm water
Skip soaps with bleach, chlorine, alcohol, moisturizers, scents or antibacterial agents
Rinse the mask in plain water. You can add plain white vinegar to the rinse water: it cuts down on smells and germs
Let the mask air dry. Keep it out of direct sunlight
Every week, hand wash the tubing and headgear with pure soap and warm water. Gently towel dry them, then let them air dry
If you use a humidifier, use distilled water and replace the water each night. Clean the humidifier as your manual says
Empty the humidifier before you move your machine, so water doesn’t spill into it

Don’t put a regular room humidifier in your bedroom: it could damage your CPAP machine’s motor. Ask your equipment provider how to keep your model clean and working well.

For the machines in the 2021 Philips recall, the advice was to stop using cleaners that use ozone or ultraviolet (UV) light, because they aren’t authorized cleaning methods

chapters.this-might-be-you.heroBody: Sleep apnea can look different in a child or a woman, and the risk grows with age. What to watch for, how children are tested and treated, and the help you can get.
chapters.this-might-be-you.focus: Seasons of life: signs in children, testing and treatment for children, a child on CPAP, later life, and women. Care and community: partners and household, helping someone, First Nations and Inuit coverage, and paying for it.
chapters.this-might-be-you.vibe: Warm and practical: for the person who notices, and the person who helps.
chapters.this-might-be-you.categoriesInt: Sleep apnea doesn’t look the same for everyone

Sleep apnea can look different in children and in women, and the risk grows with age. Often it’s a parent, partner or family member who notices first. This chapter helps you know what to look for and who to ask. It is not a way to diagnose anyone.
chapters.this-might-be-you.startHere.hea: A season of life, or someone you care for?
Sleep apnea affects 1 to 5 children in 100. Some children snore but don’t have sleep apnea
At night: snoring (steady, with pauses, or only in some positions), breathing only through the mouth, long pauses in breathing, waking often, and sweating
Restless sleep can look like turning from side to side, jerking the legs, or sitting up to breathe better while still asleep

During the day: sleepiness, especially at school or in quiet activities, trouble learning or concentrating, low energy for sports and hobbies, and irritability, hyperactivity, impulsivity or aggression

The most common cause is large tonsils or adenoids. This often happens between ages 2 and 8. Extra weight, weak breathing muscles, the shape of the skull and jaw, and other health conditions can also cause it
Other signs parents notice include bed-wetting, night terrors, and unusual sleep positions, such as the head tipped back or sitting up with the mouth open
Finding it early matters. Untreated, it can be linked to high blood pressure, poor growth, learning difficulties and behaviour problems
These signs are not a diagnosis. If you notice them, talk to your child’s doctor. Snoring and long pauses while your child sleeps are worth mentioning.
Start with your child’s doctor. They will usually refer your child to a sleep medicine specialist at a hospital
An overnight sleep study in a sleep lab (polysomnography) is the standard test for children. There is no replacement for it at this time

During the study, small wires are attached to the skin with paste and child-friendly tape. They don’t hurt. They record oxygen, breathing, heartbeat and sleep, and a sleep technologist watches through the night
A home sleep test may be a second option for otherwise healthy children over 5, when a lab study is out of reach because of long waits, distance or cost
Overnight oximetry (a finger sensor that measures oxygen) and questionnaires can help, but they shouldn’t be used alone to diagnose sleep apnea in children
Lab studies are hard to get in many parts of Canada, and waits can delay treatment. Ask your child’s doctor what the wait is where you live
Your child’s sleep specialist looks at the results to find what kind of sleep problem it is and how serious it is.
Which sleep test is right for my child?
How long is the wait, and where is the nearest lab?
What should we bring to the sleep study?
Who will explain the results to us?
Surgery to remove the tonsils and adenoids (adenotonsillectomy) is often the first treatment, because large tonsils and adenoids are often the cause
Other treatments include a weight program if your child carries extra weight, medicines to reduce swelling in the nose or airway, and less exposure to second-hand smoke and other pollution
Some children need CPAP, a machine that blows air through a mask to keep the airway open. Some still need it after other treatments

After this surgery, children with sleep apnea are watched more closely in hospital. Most go home after one night. Children under 3 with other conditions, such as Down syndrome, are more likely to have breathing problems after surgery
Your child may need a follow-up sleep study after treatment

Once your child is home after surgery, call your child’s surgeon, clinic or doctor right away for a fever of 38.5°C or higher, vomiting that won’t stop, pain that gets worse, refusing to drink, or fresh blood in the nose or mouth
If your child is bleeding or having trouble breathing, take them to the closest emergency department right away
If your child has other health conditions, the sleep team may also bring in other specialists. Tonsil surgery isn’t used to treat snoring alone in children.
Your child’s sleep team follows your child’s care. A sleep study sets the pressure on the machine, and another study after starting checks that it’s working and whether the pressure needs to change
Your child needs a mask made for children (a paediatric mask), fitted and tried on, not an adult mask
CPAP and follow-up care are different for children. Get help from professionals who work with children
Your child can practise wearing the mask for short times during the day, during a quiet activity they enjoy
Most children need time to get used to it. Make it part of the bedtime routine. A sticker chart or other reward can help
Don’t fasten the mask too tightly. Check your child’s face for pressure marks
CPAP is for every night of sleep, including holidays, sleepovers and camping
If your child is sick and you’re worried about their breathing, call your child’s health-care provider or have your child seen at your local emergency department

Children’s CPAP gives one steady pressure, set by the sleep team. Auto-adjusting machines are not for children. Some masks with magnets, including a youth version of one mask, have had Health Canada warnings: see Partners and household.
In 2016 and 2017, 12.8% of Canadians aged 60 to 79 said they had been diagnosed with sleep apnea. That’s three times the rate in adults aged 18 to 59
Adults aged 40 to 79 are at higher risk than younger adults. Being over 40 is one of the risk factors
As you get older, or if you gain weight, habits that helped before may stop being enough. If your symptoms come back, see your doctor
If you gain or lose 30 pounds or more, see your doctor. Your treatment may need to be checked
Before sedation or anesthesia, for a dental procedure, a test or surgery, tell everyone caring for you that you have sleep apnea
Use your CPAP or dental device everywhere you sleep, including an overnight stay in hospital. A medical alert bracelet that says you have sleep apnea can help
In Ontario, residents of long-term care homes can get Assistive Devices Program funding for a PAP machine
These numbers come from a national health survey. They describe Canadians in general, not any one person.
Women: the signs can look different
In a 2016–2017 national survey, men were twice as likely as women to say they had been diagnosed with sleep apnea
Men more often have the classic signs, such as loud snoring or someone seeing them stop breathing
Women more often feel tired or sleepy in the day, or have trouble falling or staying asleep
Because the signs differ, sleep apnea may be missed in women
Always tired, or sleeping badly, and not sure why? Ask your doctor whether sleep apnea could be part of it. See Is It Sleep Apnea? for the signs.
Bed partners and family often notice the signs first. Many people with sleep apnea don’t know they snore or gasp for breath at night
Once your partner is treated, you may sleep better too

Some CPAP masks have magnets in the clips or straps. Their magnetic field may affect how some metal implants and objects in the body work, or move them. Examples are pacemakers, metal stents and metal in the eye. This may cause serious injury

For the masks in Health Canada’s 2022 advisory, the advice is to stop using the mask if you, anyone in your household, a caregiver or a bed partner has one of the listed implants, and to get a mask with no magnets. For other masks with magnets, check with the mask’s maker and your health care team
A later Health Canada recall of other masks with magnets warned that interference could affect how an implant works or where it sits, with a risk of serious injury or death
Each machine is set for the person using it. Using a machine set for someone else could harm your health

Does anyone in your home have a pacemaker, defibrillator, cochlear implant, metal stent, clip or plate, or any other implant? Check whether your mask has magnets, and check with the mask’s maker and your health care team before you use it.
If someone you love snores with pauses or gasps in their sleep, and is very sleepy in the day, encourage them to see their doctor
Learn about their prescribed treatment, and help them get used to it
Encourage them to keep going. Getting comfortable with a mask can take a few weeks, or even months
Reassure them that using CPAP doesn’t change how you feel about them
Support their efforts to be active, lose weight or quit smoking
Helping a parent? Before a hospital stay or sedation, make sure the care team knows they have sleep apnea, and pack their machine
Women more often have tiredness or trouble sleeping as signs, so listen to how they feel, not only to how they sound
Falling asleep at the wheel, or a near miss, can’t wait. See the warning signs at the top of Driving & Staying Safe.
First Nations and Inuit: NIHB coverage
The Non-Insured Health Benefits (NIHB) program covers CPAP and auto CPAP machines, masks and supplies for eligible First Nations and Inuit. Prior approval is needed

You can be eligible if you live in Canada and are a First Nations person registered under the Indian Act, an Inuk recognized by an Inuit land claim organization, or a child under 2 whose parent is eligible

Some people get these benefits through a First Nations or Inuit government, community or health authority instead, such as clients of the First Nations Health Authority in BC. Not sure? Contact your NIHB regional office

The request needs a diagnosis of sleep apnea with symptoms, your sleep study results and a prescription. It can start with a rental of up to 3 months, or with a request to buy. Buying needs test results that show your sleep improved on the machine
NIHB’s replacement guidelines allow up to: a machine every 5 years, and 2 masks with headgear, 2 tubes and 14 inlet filters a year. Each replacement needs a new prescription

Equipment comes from an enrolled respiratory provider with a registered respiratory therapist, or a registered nurse trained in managing respiratory conditions, on staff. The price covers mask fitting, set-up, follow-up and teaching
NIHB doesn’t cover the cost of the sleep test itself
Coverage is only for goods and services you get in Canada. Show your provider your client identification so they can confirm your coverage.
Coverage for First Nations and Inuit is being reviewed with an Indigenous health partner and will appear here soon. Until then, contact your NIHB regional office.
chapters.this-might-be-you.categories.10: You can claim a CPAP machine bought with a prescription as a medical expense on your income tax return
Many insurance plans cover CPAP equipment prescribed by a sleep doctor. Your insurer will ask for a copy of your prescription
Public coverage differs by province. For example, Alberta’s public health insurance doesn’t currently pay for CPAP equipment, while Ontario has a program that helps pay for a machine

In Ontario, the Assistive Devices Program pays 75% of its price for a PAP machine, or 100% if you get Ontario Works, the Ontario Disability Support Program or Assistance for Children with Severe Disabilities. It doesn’t pay for replacement masks or headgear

paths.cpap.title: CPAP
paths.cpap.heroBody: From your prescription to your first weeks, then cleaning, supplies and travel: the cards that matter most with CPAP, in one order.
paths.cpap.intro.heading: Living with CPAP
paths.cpap.intro.body.1: CPAP is generally the most effective treatment for obstructive sleep apnea, and the most common type of PAP. A machine blows air through a tube into a mask, and the airflow helps keep your airway open while you sleep. A CPAP machine gives one steady pressure. An APAP machine adjusts the pressure through the night as your breathing changes. You need a prescription, and your prescriber sets your settings.
paths.cpap.intro.body.2: CPAP is a treatment, not a cure: it only works when you use it. Getting used to it can take up to 6 weeks, and a good mask fit is the key. This path follows the order most people need: your options, driving, your setup and first weeks, then cleaning, supplies and travel. Expect follow-up soon after you start, then every year.

paths.bilevel.heroBody: What bilevel is, who prescribes it, and the setup and everyday cards that apply: in one order.
paths.bilevel.intro.heading: Living with bilevel
paths.bilevel.intro.body.1: A bilevel (BiPAP) machine gives a higher pressure when you breathe in and a lower pressure when you breathe out. It’s more complex than CPAP, and a sleep specialist should prescribe it. It’s also used for some other breathing problems in sleep, when oxygen and carbon dioxide levels don’t improve with CPAP. Your sleep specialist decides whether it’s right for you, and why.
paths.bilevel.intro.body.2: This path starts with what bilevel is and when a specialist uses it. Central sleep apnea needs a specialist’s assessment, because standard machines used alone can make it worse. Then come the setup, safety and everyday cards. Only trained professionals should change your machine’s settings.

paths.travel-cpap.title: Travel CPAP
paths.travel-cpap.heroBody: Taking your treatment with you: travel machines, flying, power, and keeping your routine away from home.
paths.travel-cpap.intro.heading: CPAP away from home
paths.travel-cpap.intro.body.1: Sleep apnea doesn’t take a holiday. CPAP only works when you use it, so take it with you when you travel. A smaller travel machine is easy to carry, quiet, and can run on batteries. The trade-offs: the pressure may not stay as steady, batteries cost extra where there’s no power supply, and it may not humidify the air enough. A travel machine still needs a prescription, and it must be set for you.
paths.travel-cpap.intro.body.2: When you fly in Canada, your CPAP can go in your carry-on, and its distilled water is exempt from the liquid limits at screening. You don’t need a doctor’s note for screening, though one can help. Altitude can change how some machines work. If you live in, or often travel to, places much higher or lower than where your treatment was set up, ask your prescriber and equipment provider about it.

paths.oral-appliance.title: Oral appliance
paths.oral-appliance.heroBody: A mouth device for sleep apnea: who it may suit, what to check first, and how it compares.
paths.oral-appliance.intro.heading: Treating sleep apnea with an oral appliance
paths.oral-appliance.intro.body.1: An oral appliance fits over your upper and lower teeth and moves your lower jaw forward. That brings your tongue forward and opens your airway. It may suit mild to moderate sleep apnea, or people who can’t use or don’t want CPAP. For people it works for, a custom device can work as well as CPAP and is often easier to put up with.
paths.oral-appliance.intro.body.2: Everyone needs a medical assessment first, to confirm sleep apnea and how severe it is, and your dentist works with your doctor. Boil-and-bite devices are not recommended for treating sleep apnea. After you start, your doctor may send you for a follow-up sleep test to check it’s working.

paths.children.title: Children
paths.children.heroBody: Snoring, pauses and restless sleep in a child: the signs, how children are tested, and the treatments.
paths.children.intro.heading: Sleep apnea in children
paths.children.intro.body.1: Children can have obstructive sleep apnea too. Their airway keeps closing, partly or completely, while they sleep. Signs at night include snoring, breathing only through the mouth, restless sleep and long pauses in breathing. In the day, a child may be sleepy, find it hard to concentrate, or be irritable or hyperactive. Some children snore but don’t have sleep apnea.
paths.children.intro.body.2: A sleep study is how it’s diagnosed. For children, an overnight study in a lab is the standard. A home test is a second choice, only for otherwise healthy children over 5 who can’t get a lab study, and overnight oximetry shouldn’t be used alone. Large tonsils or adenoids are a common cause. Treatment can include surgery to remove them, a weight loss program if your child is overweight, medicines to reduce swelling, or CPAP. Your child’s sleep team decides with you.

paths.not-diagnosed-yet.title: Not diagnosed yet
paths.not-diagnosed-yet.heroBody: Wondering if it’s sleep apnea? The signs, how testing works, and what to ask your doctor.
paths.not-diagnosed-yet.intro.heading: Before a diagnosis
paths.not-diagnosed-yet.intro.body.1: Many people with sleep apnea don’t know they have it. In population surveys, 86% to 95% of people with significant sleep apnea had never been diagnosed. A bed partner or family member often notices the signs first: loud snoring, or pauses in breathing with gasping or choking. Being very sleepy during the day is the most common sign.
paths.not-diagnosed-yet.intro.body.2: Only a sleep study can tell whether you have sleep apnea, in a lab or at home. Home tests aren’t for checking people who have no symptoms. Start by seeing your family doctor or nurse practitioner. Untreated sleep apnea raises the risk of a car crash. If you’ve nodded off at the wheel, or nearly, read Stop and act now in Driving & Staying Safe first.
