funding.groups.nihb: First Nations and Inuit health benefits
funding.programs.fed-nihb-respiratory.co: NIHB covers CPAP and auto CPAP (APAP) machines, and bilevel machines for some people. It also covers masks with headgear, tubing, chin straps and inlet filters. The usual limits are one machine every 5 years, 2 masks with headgear a year for each type, 2 tubes a year, 2 chin straps a year and 14 inlet filters a year. More may be considered case by case.
funding.programs.fed-nihb-respiratory.wh: First Nations people registered under the Indian Act, Inuit recognized by an Inuit land claim organization, and children under 2 whose parent is eligible, living in Canada. Some First Nations and Inuit get their benefits directly from their own government, community or health authority instead. You need a diagnosis of sleep apnea with symptoms, a sleep study read by a sleep doctor and a prescription. A Level 1, Level 3 (home) or Level 4 study is accepted.
funding.programs.fed-nihb-respiratory.ho: Your machine needs prior approval before you get it, and so do masks, tubing and chin straps. Your provider sends the request to the NIHB regional office for its region. Providers registered with NIHB bill it directly, so you don’t pay for eligible items. If you pay yourself, check with NIHB before you buy, and send your claim within a year.
funding.programs.fed-nihb-respiratory.no: It can start with a rental of up to 3 months, or with a purchase. Buying the machine needs a treatment test that shows your sleep has improved. The price must include mask fitting, set-up, follow-up and teaching. NIHB doesn’t pay for the sleep test itself.
funding.programs.bc-fnha-mse.covered: First Nations people in BC who are clients of the First Nations Health Authority get their health benefits from its Health Benefits program, not NIHB. Its medical supplies and equipment benefit lists CPAP, auto CPAP (APAP) and bilevel machines, usually one every 5 years. It also lists masks with headgear, tubing, chin straps and inlet filters.
funding.programs.bc-fnha-mse.who: First Nations people with Indian status who live in BC, and infants up to 24 months if a parent is eligible.
funding.programs.bc-fnha-mse.howToApply: Ask your provider whether they’re registered with the program. Registered providers bill it directly. A machine needs approval first: your provider can send your sleep study, a medical note and a quote. If your provider isn’t registered, you pay and ask for a refund.
funding.programs.fed-vac-poc9.covered: Veterans Affairs Canada’s respiratory equipment benefit includes CPAP, auto CPAP (APAP) and bilevel (BiPAP) machines. Equipment and supplies that may be approved are listed in its benefit grids.
funding.programs.fed-vac-poc9.who: Eligible Veterans Affairs Canada clients. For a condition that isn’t linked to your disability benefits, it may pay what’s left after your provincial health plan, or what that plan doesn’t provide.
funding.programs.fed-vac-poc9.howToApply: Veterans Affairs Canada pays for the item or pays you back. If your provider charges more than it can pay, you can choose another provider or pay the difference. Send claims within 18 months.
funding.programs.fed-cra-medical.covered: A CPAP machine counts as an eligible medical expense on your income tax return. It needs a prescription.
funding.programs.fed-cra-medical.who: You, or your spouse or common-law partner, can claim amounts paid in any 12-month period ending in the tax year.
funding.programs.fed-cra-medical.howToAp: Only the part above a yearly threshold counts. For 2025 returns, that’s the lesser of 3% of your net income or $2,834. Keep your receipts and your prescription. In Quebec, provincial credits are claimed through Revenu Québec.
funding.programs.on-adp-respiratory.cove: Ontario’s Assistive Devices Program helps pay for a CPAP, auto CPAP (APAP) or bilevel (BPAP) machine. The machine package includes a heated humidifier, a basic mask and headgear, a carrying case, tubing, filters and a user manual. The program pays 75% of its approved price, and you pay the other 25%. If you get Ontario Works, the Ontario Disability Support Program or Assistance for Children with Severe Disabilities, it pays 100%.
funding.programs.on-adp-respiratory.who: Ontario residents with a valid health card who need the machine for 6 months or longer. A doctor at a sleep clinic registered with the program assesses you. The assessment must include a Level 1 sleep study at a sleep lab registered with the program. Your income isn’t considered.
funding.programs.on-adp-respiratory.howT: Follow the program’s steps before you buy. Get assessed, then buy from a business registered with the program. The business sends in the form for you. The program pays its share to that business, and you pay your 25% when you pick up the machine. If you buy before the steps are done, you pay the full cost.
funding.programs.on-adp-respiratory.note: It doesn’t pay for replacement masks or headgear, repairs or oral appliances. The program expects a machine to last at least 5 years. You can apply to replace it if your needs change, or if it’s worn out, out of warranty and can’t be repaired at a reasonable cost. Residents of long-term care homes can get funding for a PAP machine. You don’t qualify if you already get, or qualify for, the same equipment through WSIB, or through Veterans Affairs Canada as a Group “A” veteran.
funding.programs.on-odsp-msn.covered: If you get the Ontario Disability Support Program, its Mandatory Special Necessities benefit can cover replacement PAP supplies: masks, mask cushions and liners, interfaces with headgear, tubing, water chambers, filters and distilled water. Its list also includes an oral appliance for sleep apnea.
funding.programs.on-odsp-msn.who: ODSP recipients and members of their benefit unit, diagnosed with obstructive sleep apnea. An approved health care professional confirms the diagnosis and how long you’ll need the supplies.
funding.programs.on-odsp-msn.howToApply: Ask your ODSP office for supplies when you need them. ODSP must approve the need first. It pays a supplier who bills it, or adds the amount to your monthly payment. It pays actual costs, based on receipts. Approval is for basic items at the most economical cost.
funding.programs.on-odsp-msn.notes: The machine itself comes through the Assistive Devices Program. ODSP pays only if no other program or private insurance pays for the same item.
funding.programs.sk-sail-cpap.covered: Saskatchewan lends you a CPAP machine through SAIL for a $275 program fee. The fee covers the loan and any repairs needed during the machine’s useful life of 5 years. You can keep the machine longer if it still works well. You pay the fee before you get the machine. There are no payment plans, and the fee isn’t refundable.
funding.programs.sk-sail-cpap.who: Saskatchewan residents with a valid health services number and moderate to severe sleep apnea (an AHI or RDI of 15 or higher). Also children under 18 who need CPAP for a medical condition. A Sleep Disorder Centre can also prescribe it for an urgent medical need, or for mild sleep apnea with symptoms in someone who works in a high-risk job. SAIL isn’t for people who get benefits from another government agency, such as SGI, the Workers’ Compensation Board, NIHB or Veterans Affairs Canada.
funding.programs.sk-sail-cpap.howToApply: Your family doctor refers you to a respirologist. You need a Level 1 or Level 3 sleep study, and a Level 3 study must be done in Saskatchewan unless SAIL approves otherwise. A sleep specialist at a Saskatchewan Sleep Disorders Centre reads the results and confirms the diagnosis. A Saskatchewan respirologist prescribes CPAP, and can apply for you or tell you how.
funding.programs.sk-sail-cpap.notes: You pay for your own supplies, such as masks, headgear and filters. With Supplementary Health Benefits, or Family Health Benefits for children, the machine and supplies are free. SAIL doesn’t pay you back for a machine you bought yourself, and it doesn’t offer travel machines. You can have one SAIL machine at a time.
funding.programs.mb-misericordia-cpap.co: Manitoba’s CPAP program helps pay for a machine. After a successful trial you pay a $500 co-pay, which includes the machine, your first mask, filters, a humidifier chamber and tubing. The health authority pays the rest of the machine’s cost, plus a first consultation with your supplier, mask fitting, teaching and follow-up visits for treatment problems.
funding.programs.mb-misericordia-cpap.wh: Manitobans prescribed a CPAP machine by the Sleep Disorder Centre at Misericordia Health Centre.
funding.programs.mb-misericordia-cpap.ho: Take your prescription to one of the two suppliers the Sleep Disorder Centre lists. The supplier fits you, teaches you how to use the equipment and gives you a trial of at least a month. To pass the trial, you use it on at least 70% of nights, for 4 hours or more. That’s the program’s rule; your sleep team sets your own goal.
funding.programs.mb-misericordia-cpap.no: After that, you pay for supplies, delivery and repairs. You can get a new machine every 5 years for another $500 co-pay. If you can’t afford it and have no Employment and Income Assistance or private insurance, ask about exceptional circumstances.
funding.programs.bc-bcea-breathing.cover: If you get income or disability assistance in BC, the ministry may pay for a CPAP or bilevel machine for moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea. If you can’t use one, it may pay for a mandibular advancement device instead. It may replace the machine after 5 years, and the supplies needed to run it after 1 year.
funding.programs.bc-bcea-breathing.who: People on income or disability assistance who are eligible for general health supplements, or who meet the life-threatening health needs criteria. No other resource, such as another program or private insurance, can pay. It must be the least expensive suitable device.
funding.programs.bc-bcea-breathing.howTo: Get a quote from a supplier. Fill in the Breathing Device Request and Justification form (HR3727) with a doctor’s or nurse practitioner’s prescription and a respiratory therapist’s assessment. The ministry must approve it before you buy.
funding.programs.bc-bcea-breathing.notes: It won’t pay for a device bought without approval, unless it’s a life-threatening emergency. It may share the cost when insurance pays only part.
funding.programs.ab-aish.covered: AISH may help with the cost of a CPAP device and supplies, as a health-related personal benefit.
funding.programs.ab-aish.who: AISH clients with no more than $5,000 in non-exempt assets, or in financial hardship, who need the benefit, aren’t eligible for it through any other program or source, and meet that benefit’s own requirements.
funding.programs.ab-aish.howToApply: Talk to your AISH worker before you buy. Some personal benefits may need to be paid back.
funding.programs.nb-sd-respiratory.cover: New Brunswick’s respiratory program covers CPAP machines up to $1,800 and BPAP machines up to $3,150, and CPAP and BPAP masks and supplies.
funding.programs.nb-sd-respiratory.who: Clients of the Department of Social Development and their dependents, and people with special health needs who qualify for assisted health care. You need a Health Services card that shows this coverage. For full benefits, you can’t have any other coverage for the item.
funding.programs.nb-sd-respiratory.howTo: Use the program’s CPAP or BPAP application form.
funding.programs.nb-sd-respiratory.notes: How often you can replace a machine varies. Supplies may be paid monthly, and quantities are monitored.
funding.province.bc-not-covered.title: In BC, PharmaCare and the Medical Services Plan don’t pay for CPAP
funding.province.bc-not-covered.body: BC PharmaCare doesn’t cover CPAP machines. BC’s Medical Services Plan doesn’t pay for PAP machines or accessories. Private or extended health insurance often covers some or all of a prescribed machine. If you get income or disability assistance, see the ministry’s breathing devices benefit below. First Nations people may get help through the First Nations Health Authority.
funding.province.ab-not-covered.title: In Alberta, public health insurance doesn’t pay for CPAP
funding.province.ab-not-covered.body: Alberta Health Care Insurance doesn’t cover CPAP equipment or accessories. Health insurance may cover it. These programs may also help: Alberta Income Support, Special Needs Assistance for Seniors, AISH, NIHB and Veterans Affairs Canada.
funding.province.qc-still-checking.title: Quebec: we’re still checking
funding.province.qc-still-checking.body: We haven’t confirmed a public program for CPAP machines in Quebec. In figures published in 2024, 74% of people diagnosed with sleep apnea in Quebec had private insurance, and 3.1% had social assistance that partly covers the machine. Some had no coverage and could only claim the medical expense tax credit. We’re checking whether a public program has started since.
funding.province.stillChecking.title: {province}: we’re still checking
funding.province.stillChecking.body: We haven’t found and checked an official {province} program for CPAP yet, so we aren’t listing one. That doesn’t mean there’s no help. Ask your sleep clinic or doctor, and look at the federal programs below.
funding.province.aadl.title: Alberta Aids to Daily Living: we’re still checking
funding.province.aadl.body: We couldn’t read Alberta Aids to Daily Living’s rules for CPAP, so we aren’t listing it yet. Ask your sleep clinic or doctor.
funding.liivv.askUsBody: Liivv doesn’t bill any program directly yet. When you order supplies from us, you pay for your order. Some programs pay you back from a receipt. Others pay only a business registered with them. Check how yours pays before you order, or ask us.
machineGuide.title: Common sleep apnea machines, compared
machineGuide.notSold: Liivv doesn’t sell CPAP or other sleep apnea machines yet.
machineGuide.intro: This guide helps you talk to your prescriber about the machines in it. It doesn’t recommend one.
machineGuide.cards.1.title: Machine types, and who prescribes each
machineGuide.cards.1.items.1: A CPAP machine blows air at one steady pressure
machineGuide.cards.1.items.2: An auto CPAP (APAP) changes the pressure through the night as your breathing pattern changes
machineGuide.cards.1.items.3: A bilevel (BiPAP) machine uses a higher pressure when you breathe in and a lower one when you breathe out
machineGuide.cards.1.items.4: Some bilevel machines are more advanced and are made for complex breathing disorders. They aren’t needed for obstructive sleep apnea. ASV is one of these (see the ASV card)
machineGuide.cards.1.items.5: Every machine needs a prescription. Some provincial guidance says auto and bilevel machines should be prescribed only by a sleep specialist
machineGuide.cards.1.items.6: Each CPAP machine must be set for the person using it, and only trained professionals should change machine settings
machineGuide.cards.2.title: Travel machines
machineGuide.cards.2.items.1: Travel machines are easier to take with you, and some run on a battery
machineGuide.cards.2.items.2: The trade-offs: pressure may not be as steady, batteries cost extra when there’s no wall power, and they may not give enough humidity
machineGuide.cards.2.items.3: Altitude can change how a machine works unless it has features that adjust for it. Talk about portability and altitude with your prescriber and your equipment supplier
machineGuide.cards.2.items.4: If you plan to use your machine on the plane, tell the airline’s reservation agent whether it uses batteries or needs onboard power
machineGuide.cards.2.items.5: When you fly, bring your machine as carry-on with a letter from your doctor, and check the type of power supply where you’re going
machineGuide.cards.2.items.6: Some travel machines take only their own masks and parts, so check before you buy a mask
machineGuide.cards.3.title: Data and apps
machineGuide.cards.3.items.1: Many machines record how many hours you use them, breathing events and mask leak
machineGuide.cards.3.items.2: Some connect to a phone app by Bluetooth, Wi-Fi or cellular, so you can track your data and send reports to your provider. Others store reports on an SD or USB card, if you’d rather not use a wireless connection
machineGuide.cards.3.items.3: Many machines store data on servers outside Canada, where privacy laws may differ. Ask your provider how they report your data and how they keep it safe
machineGuide.cards.3.note: The chart shows how each machine shares data.
machineGuide.cards.4.title: Recalls and safety
machineGuide.cards.4.items.1: PAP machines sold in Canada must have a Health Canada medical device licence. You can look up a model in Health Canada’s Medical Devices Active Licence Listing (MDALL), and check Health Canada’s website for recalls
machineGuide.cards.4.items.2: The Philips foam recall (RA-62729) covers several Philips CPAP and bilevel machines and ventilators made before April 26, 2021. If you have one, talk to your doctor or equipment provider before you stop or change how you use it
machineGuide.cards.4.items.3: Clean it only as the maker’s instructions say. Cleaning methods that haven’t been validated, such as ozone, could add to the foam breakdown
machineGuide.cards.4.note: The licences in this guide were checked on 2026-10-13. Licences and recalls change, so check again before you buy.
machineGuide.cards.5.title: Questions to ask before you buy
machineGuide.cards.5.items.1: Is this the type of machine my prescriber ordered, and is it right for my condition?
machineGuide.cards.5.items.2: Does it have a Health Canada licence, and has it been recalled?
machineGuide.cards.5.items.3: Is it new or used, and is there a warranty? Equipment bought in Canada usually has a 3-year warranty and should have a CSA stamp
machineGuide.cards.5.items.4: Will the seller ask for my prescription before selling it to me?
machineGuide.cards.5.items.5: Who sets it up, follows up with me, and handles repairs?
machineGuide.cards.5.items.6: Can I try it first? Some suppliers offer trials, and some don’t give returns or refunds once equipment has been used
machineGuide.cards.5.items.7: With a second-hand machine, it can be hard to know if it works well and if any warranty is left
machineGuide.cards.5.note: Talk to your doctor before and after you buy.
machineGuide.cards.asv.title: ASV
machineGuide.cards.asv.items.1: ASV is a type of bilevel machine. Some provincial guidance says bilevel machines should be prescribed only by a sleep specialist
machineGuide.cards.asv.items.2: People with suspected central sleep apnea should be checked with a detailed overnight test in a sleep lab to find the right treatment
machineGuide.cards.asv.items.3: In 2015, Health Canada posted a Type I recall of several ASV machines. It names a serious safety concern for people with symptomatic, chronic heart failure with reduced left ventricular ejection fraction who are on ASV therapy: a 33.5% increased risk of cardiovascular death
